title: Conversations and Presentations
bigQuestion: How do you talk so that people understand you, and listen so that you understand them?

story.title: Was the Ending Fair?
story.kicker: A book club of five fourth graders takes on an old tale, and the argument gets loud before it gets good.
paragraphs: Ms. Nakamura's book club sits in a circle on the rug. This week they read a very old story by Hans Christian Andersen, first printed in 1837, about a little mermaid. In the tale, the mermaid trades her voice to a sea witch for a pair of human legs. She hopes the prince will love her. He marries someone else. She is given a chance to save herself by harming him, and she refuses. At dawn she turns into foam on the sea.

Jamal starts. "That ending was not fair. She gave up everything and got nothing." Sofia jumps in before he finishes. "No, it was fair, she chose it!" Then three people talk at once. Nobody can hear anybody. Ms. Nakamura holds up one hand and waits. The circle goes quiet.

"Let's try that again," she says. "One person at a time. And before you answer, say back what the last person said." Jamal goes first, slowly. Sofia says, "Jamal thinks the ending was unfair because she gave up so much. I see that. But I think choosing not to hurt the prince was her own choice, and that makes it hers." Jamal nods. "Okay. But could you read me the part where she chooses? I want to hear it again."

Sofia finds the page and reads it aloud. Marcus, who has not spoken yet, says, "What if the story is not about whether she wins? What if it is about what kind of person she is?" The circle gets quiet in a different way. Everyone is thinking.

By the end, nobody has changed their vote. Jamal still says unfair. Sofia still says fair. But each one can explain the other side now. Ms. Nakamura writes on the board: Listen. Say it back. Ask. Build. This chapter is about how to talk and listen so that a conversation gets better instead of just louder.
story.think: The book club did not agree at the end. So how do you know the second try was better than the first?

lessons.title: Come Prepared
lessons.mainIdea: A good discussion starts before it starts: read the text, mark what you noticed, and bring one thing to say.
reading: Sofia came to book club with a sticky note on page 30. It marked the moment the mermaid throws the knife into the sea. When Jamal asked to hear that part, she found it in five seconds. That is what it looks like to *prepare*. She did the work before the circle formed.

Preparing for a discussion means three things. Read the whole text, not just the first pages. Mark places that surprised you, confused you or made you feel something. Then write down one thing you want to say and one question you want to ask. That is enough. You do not need a speech.

Being prepared changes how you feel in the circle. You are not scrambling. You are not hoping nobody calls on you. You have something to give. And when someone says, Where does it say that?, you can put your finger on the page.

words.d: to get ready ahead of time by reading, marking and planning what to say
a talk where a group shares ideas about one topic and listens to each other

look.title: Two Sticky Notes
look.text: Before book club, Marcus put two sticky notes in his book. One says: Page 12, she cannot talk anymore. Why did she agree to that? The other says: Page 30, I did not expect her to throw the knife. When the circle starts, he has a question and a surprise ready. Jamal has no notes and is flipping pages looking for the part he means.
look.prompt: Who is more likely to help the discussion move forward, and why? What would one sticky note have done for Jamal?

check.q: What does it mean to prepare for a discussion?
choices: Read, mark and plan one thing to say
Wait to hear what others think
check.why: Preparing means reading the whole text, marking spots and bringing one idea and one question.

check.q: Why did Sofia find the knife scene so fast?
choices: She had marked it with a sticky note
Ms. Nakamura told her the page
It was on the first page
check.why: She marked page 30 before club. Preparing means you can find the spot when someone asks.

check.q: What is a good thing to mark while reading?
choices: A part that surprised or confused you
check.why: Surprises, confusions and feelings make the best discussion spots.

lessons.title: Listen and Build On
lessons.mainIdea: Listening means taking in what someone said and connecting your idea to theirs, not just waiting for your turn.
reading: In the first try, Sofia talked before Jamal finished. In the second try, she said, Jamal thinks the ending was unfair because she gave up so much. Then she added her own idea. That is called *building on* what someone said. Her idea sat on top of his instead of knocking it over.

Real listening is not silent waiting. It is taking in the other person's words so well that you could say them back. Try these starters: I agree with Jamal because. I want to add to what Sofia said. That connects to what Marcus asked. Each one shows you heard, and each one moves the talk forward.

One more rule: eyes on the speaker, not on your own page. When you look at the person talking, you catch more than words. You catch when they are unsure. You catch when they are excited. A discussion works when people are listening to each other, not performing at each other.

words.d: to connect your idea to what someone else just said
to take in what someone says so well that you could say it back

look.title: Who Spoke in Ten Minutes
look.prompt: Two people took most of the turns. What could Jamal and Sofia do differently? What could the group say to bring in Elena?

check.q: What does it mean to build on someone's idea?
choices: Say something louder than they did
Change the subject to your idea
Connect your idea to what they just said
Repeat their idea word for word
check.why: Building on means your idea sits on top of theirs. You connect, then add.

check.q: Which sentence starter shows you were listening?
choices: I want to add to what Sofia said
I was not listening, can you repeat that
That is wrong, listen to me
check.why: 'I want to add to what Sofia said' shows you heard her and are connecting to her idea.

check.q: Why should your eyes stay on the speaker?
choices: So you look polite in the photo
So the teacher gives you a point
So you can plan what to say next
So you catch more than just the words
check.why: Watching the speaker helps you notice if they are unsure or excited, not only what they say.

lessons.title: Ask and Disagree Politely
lessons.mainIdea: Questions and polite disagreement make a discussion stronger, as long as you talk about the idea and not the person.
reading: Jamal did not give up his view. He asked Sofia to read the page again. That is a good question: it asks for *evidence*, the proof in the text. Other good questions are: What do you mean by that? Where does it say so? Why do you think that? A question is not an attack. It is an invitation.

Disagreeing is allowed. Being rude is not. Compare these. You are wrong and that is dumb. Or: I see it differently, because the story says she chose to throw the knife. The second one disagrees with the idea and gives a reason. It does not call anyone a name. That is *polite disagreement*.

Here is a pattern you can use every time. Say what you heard. Say you see it differently. Give your reason from the text. Sofia did all three in one breath, and Jamal nodded. Nobody lost. A discussion where everyone agrees in one minute is usually a discussion where nobody thought very hard.

words.d: proof, such as words from the text, that supports an idea
saying you see it differently and giving a reason, without attacking the person

look.title: The Wind and the Sun
look.text: In an old fable, the North Wind and the Sun argue about who is stronger. They pick a traveler in a coat. The Wind blows as hard as it can, and the man only pulls his coat tighter. Then the Sun shines gently. The man grows warm and takes the coat off by himself. The Sun wins without force.
look.cite: Aesop's fables, an ancient Greek tale, retold in our words
look.prompt: How is the Wind like a rude argument? How is the Sun like a polite one? Which one changed the traveler's mind?

check.q: Which is a polite way to disagree?
choices: That is dumb and you are wrong.
I see it differently, because the story says she chose.
check.why: It disagrees with the idea, gives a reason from the text, and does not attack the person.

check.q: What is evidence in a book discussion?
choices: Proof from the text, such as words on a page
check.why: Evidence is proof. In a book discussion, it is what the text actually says.

check.q: What does the fable of the Wind and the Sun suggest about arguments?
choices: Force changes minds better than warmth
Gentle reasons work better than blasting someone
check.why: The Wind blew hard and lost. The Sun was gentle and the man took his coat off himself.

lessons.title: Summarize What You Heard
lessons.mainIdea: A summary of a speaker gives the main point and the biggest reasons in your own words, in a few sentences.
reading: Jamal talked for a full minute about the ending. Then Sofia said, in one sentence, what he meant: Jamal thinks the ending was unfair because she gave up so much. That sentence is a *summary*. It is short. It is in Sofia's words. And it keeps the main point and the biggest reason.

To summarize a speaker, listen for two things. First, the main point: what does this person want me to believe or know? Second, the reasons: what did they say to back it up? Leave out the small stuff, the jokes and the side trails. Keep the point and the reasons.

A summary should be much shorter than the talk. If someone speaks for a minute, your summary might be two sentences. Say it back to the speaker if you can: So you are saying that. If they nod, you got it. If they say no, not quite, you just learned something before you argued about the wrong thing.

words.d: a short retelling of the main point and biggest reasons, in your own words
the one thing a speaker most wants you to know or believe

look.title: A Minute From Jamal
look.text: Okay so the mermaid, she gives up her voice, right, and that is like her best thing, and she gets legs but every step hurts, and then the prince does not even pick her, he picks the other girl, and she could have saved herself and she does not, and then she is just foam. So how is that fair? She did everything and got nothing.
look.prompt: Find Jamal's main point. Find his two strongest reasons. Now say the whole thing in two sentences.

check.q: What should a summary of a speaker keep?
choices: The main point and the biggest reasons
check.why: A summary keeps the point and the reasons and drops the small stuff.

check.q: About how long should a summary of a one-minute talk be?
check.why: A summary is much shorter than the talk. Two sentences is about right for one minute.

check.q: Why say your summary back to the speaker?
choices: To show you talk better than they do
To check that you understood before you respond
check.why: If they nod, you got it. If not, you learn that before you argue about the wrong thing.

lessons.title: Check What You Heard
lessons.mainIdea: When you are not sure what a speaker meant, ask a clear question instead of guessing.
reading: Marcus asked, What if the story is about what kind of person she is? Priya was not sure what he meant. She could have nodded and stayed lost. Instead she said, Do you mean the ending shows she is kind? Marcus said yes. Now Priya can answer him. That is *clarifying*: asking so that something fuzzy becomes clear.

Good clarifying questions are short and honest. Can you say that again? What do you mean by fair? Are you saying the ending was good, or that it made sense? Can you give an example? None of these are dumb. Every one of them helps the whole circle, because if you were lost, someone else was too.

Clarifying also works when the speaker is a teacher, a video or a guest. Write down the parts you did not catch. Then ask about them. A listener who asks one good question learns more than a listener who nods at everything. Nodding is not the same as understanding.

words.d: asking a question so that something unclear becomes clear
one specific case that shows what a bigger idea means

look.title: The Nod
look.text: A guest comes to class to talk about her job as a nurse. She says, Most of my day is triage. Half the class nods. Nobody knows what triage means. Elena raises her hand. What does triage mean? The nurse smiles and explains: deciding who needs help first. Now the whole class understands the rest of her talk.
look.prompt: Why did so many students nod at a word they did not know? What did Elena's question do for everyone else in the room?

check.q: What is a clarifying question?
choices: A question that asks so an unclear idea becomes clear
A question that proves the speaker wrong
A question you already know the answer to
check.why: Clarifying means making something clear. You ask because you are not sure yet.

check.q: Why is nodding not the same as understanding?
choices: You can nod and still be lost
check.why: Half the class nodded at triage without knowing the word. A nod can hide confusion.

check.q: Which is a good clarifying question?
choices: Is this going to be on the test?
Do we have to listen to this?
check.why: Asking for an example is a short, honest way to make a fuzzy idea clear.

lessons.title: Put It in Order
lessons.mainIdea: A short talk needs a clear order: tell what it is about, give two or three parts in a sequence, and end on purpose.
reading: Elena has to give a two-minute talk about her grandmother's tamales. Her first try jumps around: the steaming, then the corn husks, then back to the filling, then her cousin's birthday. Her class is lost. Her second try goes in *order*: first, the filling. Second, the wrapping. Third, the steaming. Now they can follow.

A short talk has three parts. The opening tells the audience what the talk is about in one or two sentences. The middle gives two or three main points, one at a time, in an order that makes sense. The ending says the big idea one more time, or tells why it matters. Do not just stop. End.

Words that show the order help a listener stay with you. First, next, then, finally. Another reason is. The last thing is. These are signposts. A reader can look back at a page. A listener cannot rewind you. Signposts tell them where they are and what is coming.

words.d: the sequence a talk follows so a listener can follow it: first, next, last
a word like first, next or finally that tells a listener where you are in the talk

look.title: Elena's Second Try
look.text: My grandmother makes tamales every December, and it takes all day. First, she cooks the filling in a big pot. Next, she spreads dough on corn husks and adds the filling. Then she rolls and ties each one. Finally, she steams them for an hour. When you smell them, you know it is almost Christmas.
look.prompt: Find the opening, the middle steps and the ending. Circle the signpost words. What would be lost if the steps were mixed up?

check.q: What are the three parts of a short talk?
choices: A joke, a story, a joke
An opening, a middle with main points, an ending
A question, an answer, a question
A list, a picture, a bow
check.why: The opening says what the talk is about, the middle gives the points in order, the ending closes on purpose.

check.q: Why are signpost words extra important in a talk?
choices: A listener cannot rewind you the way a reader can look back
check.why: Words like first and finally tell a listener where they are, since they cannot reread what you said.

check.q: What was wrong with Elena's first try?
choices: The parts were out of order
check.why: She jumped from steaming to husks to filling. The class could not follow the sequence.

lessons.title: Details That Help
lessons.mainIdea: A talk comes alive with a few specific details, facts and examples that support each main point.
reading: Marcus gives a talk about Lake Michigan. First try: Lake Michigan is really big and cool. That is a claim with nothing under it. Second try: Lake Michigan is so big that from a Chicago beach you cannot see the other side. It touches four states. Now the audience has something to picture. Those are *details*.

A detail is a specific fact, example or description that supports a main point. Big is not a detail. Cannot see the other side is. Each main point in your talk needs at least one detail under it. Pick the one that a listener could repeat to a friend later. That is the one that will stick.

Do not pile on. Three strong details beat ten weak ones. If a fact does not support your point, leave it out, even if you like it. And if you say a number or a name, be sure of it. A talk with one wrong fact makes the audience doubt the rest.

words.d: a specific fact, example or description that supports a main point
a statement you want the audience to believe

look.title: Details Under Each Point
look.prompt: Marcus went from zero details to two and the class could picture the lake. Jamal used nine and the class got lost. What does that tell you about how many to use?

check.q: Which one is a detail?
choices: From a Chicago beach you cannot see the other side.
check.why: It is a specific fact that a listener can picture. 'Big' and 'cool' are not specific.

check.q: How many details should each main point have?
check.why: Each point needs at least one detail under it. Three strong ones beat ten weak ones.

check.q: Why does one wrong fact hurt a whole talk?
choices: It makes the talk too long
It makes the audience doubt the rest
check.why: If the audience catches one mistake, they start to wonder what else is wrong.

lessons.title: Pace and Volume
lessons.mainIdea: Speak slowly enough to be understood, loudly enough to reach the back, and pause where a period would go.
reading: Priya knows her talk cold. She gets up and races through it in forty seconds. The class hears a blur. She sat down thinking she did fine. The words were right. The *pace*, the speed of her talking, was wrong. Nervous speakers almost always go too fast, because fast feels like it will be over sooner.

Slow down more than feels normal. What feels slow to you sounds normal to a listener. Pause at the end of each sentence, right where a period would go. Breathe there. A pause is not empty time. It is the moment your listener catches up.

Then think about *volume*, how loud you are. Do not yell. Aim your voice at the person in the back row and speak so they can hear every word. Lift your chin. Your voice goes where your face points. If your face points at the floor, your words go there too.

words.d: how fast or slow you speak
how loud or soft you speak

look.title: The Same Sentence, Three Ways
look.text: Try this out loud. Say: My grandmother makes tamales every December. Say it as fast as you can, all in one rush. Now say it at a normal talking pace. Now say it slowly, with a tiny pause after grandmother and after tamales, looking at the far wall. Notice which one you would want to hear if you were sitting in the back.
look.prompt: Which version was easiest to understand? Why do nervous speakers pick the fast one anyway?

check.q: What does pace mean?
choices: How fast or slow you speak
check.why: Pace is speed. Priya's words were right, but her pace was too fast.

check.q: Where is a good place to pause in a talk?
choices: In the middle of a word
At the end of each sentence
check.why: Pause where a period would go. That is when the listener catches up.

check.q: Why does lifting your chin help your volume?
choices: Your voice goes where your face points
The teacher can see your eyes
check.why: If your face points at the floor, your words go to the floor. Aim at the back row.

lessons.title: Pictures and Objects
lessons.mainIdea: A picture or object can show what words alone cannot, but it should help the point, not replace it.
reading: Elena brings a corn husk to her tamale talk. She holds it up when she says, she spreads dough on corn husks. Suddenly the class understands what a husk is. Nobody needed a definition. That is a *visual aid*: something the audience can see that helps them understand.

A visual aid can be a real object, a photo, a drawing, a map or a simple *chart*. Marcus showed a map of Lake Michigan touching four states. Jamal drew a dinosaur next to a school bus. It showed the size. Each one did a job that words could not do as well.

Two rules. First, the visual should help the point, not decorate it. If you cannot say what it shows, leave it out. Second, do not hide behind it. Hold it up, let people look, say what it shows, then put it down and keep talking to the audience. The aid is a helper. You are still the talk.

words.d: an object, picture, map or chart the audience can see that helps them understand a point
a simple picture that shows numbers or facts so they are easy to compare

look.title: Which One Helps?
look.text: Jamal is choosing a visual for his dinosaur talk. Option one: a drawing of a Tyrannosaurus next to a school bus, showing they are about the same length. Option two: a cool dinosaur sticker with flames on it. Option three: a photo of himself at the museum with his thumb up. His main point is that some dinosaurs were as long as a bus.
look.prompt: Which visual actually helps the main point? What do the other two do instead?

check.q: What is a visual aid?
choices: Something the audience can see that helps a point
A note card you read from
check.why: A husk, a map or a drawing is something the audience sees that helps them understand.

check.q: Why did Elena's corn husk work so well?
choices: It showed what words alone could not show as fast
check.why: Seeing the husk explained the word in one second. That is what a good visual does.

check.q: What should you do after holding up a visual?
choices: Keep it in front of your face
Pass it around and stop talking
Put it away before anyone sees it
Say what it shows, then keep talking to the audience
check.why: The aid is a helper. Show it, explain it, then come back to your audience.

lessons.title: Record and Listen Back
lessons.mainIdea: Recording yourself and listening back shows you what your audience hears, so you can fix it before it counts.
reading: Priya records her talk on a tablet and plays it back. She is shocked. She says um eleven times. She rushes the ending. She says like every few seconds. None of that felt real while she was talking. Now she can hear it. A *recording* shows you what your audience hears, not what you meant.

Listen back for four things. Pace: are you racing? Volume: can you hear every word? Fillers: um, like, you know, so. And the ending: did you end on purpose or just stop? Write down one thing to fix. Just one. Record again. Then pick the next thing.

It feels strange to hear your own voice. Everybody hates it the first time. That feeling passes, and what is left is the fastest way to get better at speaking that there is. Athletes watch film. Singers listen to takes. Speakers listen back.

words.d: a saved copy of your voice or video that you can play back
a sound or word like um or like that fills space while you think

look.title: Priya's Fillers, Three Takes
look.unit: ums and likes in a two-minute talk
look.prompt: Priya fixed only one thing between takes. What do the numbers suggest about the value of listening back?

check.q: Why record yourself giving a talk?
choices: To hear what your audience hears
check.why: A recording shows you what the audience hears, not what you meant to sound like.

check.q: What is a filler?
choices: A detail that supports a point
A sound like um that fills space while you think
check.why: Um, like and you know are fillers. They take up space without saying anything.

check.q: How many things should you fix between recordings?
check.why: Pick one thing, fix it, record again. Priya's ums dropped from eleven to two that way.

lessons.title: Audience and Purpose
lessons.mainIdea: Who is listening and why you are talking should change your words, your details and your tone.
reading: Elena gives her tamale talk twice. Once to her class. Once to a room of kindergartners. To her class she says, the dough is made from corn that has been soaked and ground. To the little kids she says, the dough is soft and yellow, like play dough you can eat. Same talk. Different *audience*. Different words.

The audience is who is listening. Before you speak, ask: What do they already know? What do they care about? Kindergartners do not know what ground corn is. Your class does. A room of parents wants something different again. Change your words and details to fit the people in front of you.

The *purpose* is why you are talking. To teach how tamales are made? To make people laugh? To convince the principal to have a tamale day? Each purpose changes what you say first and what you leave out. A speaker who knows the audience and the purpose has already won half the room.

words.d: the people who are listening to you
the reason you are speaking: to teach, to entertain or to convince

look.title: One Topic, Three Rooms
look.text: Marcus has to talk about Lake Michigan three times. First, to first graders during buddy reading. Second, to his own class for a science grade. Third, to the school board, asking for a field trip to the lakefront. Same lake. Three rooms. In one room he needs simple words. In one he needs facts. In one he needs a reason they should say yes.
look.prompt: Match each room to what it needs. What one fact about the lake would you use for each audience?

check.q: What is an audience?
check.why: The audience is who is listening. Their age and knowledge change your words.

check.q: Why did Elena change 'ground corn' to 'like play dough you can eat'?
choices: Her audience was kindergartners who did not know ground corn
check.why: Kindergartners do not know what ground corn is. She picked words they could picture.

check.q: Which is a purpose for a talk?
choices: To convince the principal to have a tamale day
check.why: Purpose is the reason you speak. Convincing the principal is a reason.

review.q: What made the book club's second try better than the first?
choices: People listened, said back and asked questions
Ms. Nakamura told them the answer
They stopped talking about the book
review.why: Nobody changed their vote, but each person could explain the other side. Listening did that.

review.q: What is the best way to prepare for a book discussion?
choices: Read it all, mark spots and bring one question
Wait and see what others say
review.why: Preparing means reading the whole text, marking places and bringing something to say.

choices: I see it differently because the text says she chose.
I disagree and I will not say why.
review.why: It disagrees with the idea and gives a reason from the text without attacking anyone.

review.q: A speaker talks for one minute. What should your summary keep?
choices: Their main point and biggest reasons
review.why: A summary is short, in your words, and keeps the point and the reasons.

review.q: Which words are signposts in a talk?
review.why: First, next and finally tell a listener where they are in the order of the talk.

review.q: Nervous speakers usually talk too fast. What should they do?
choices: Slow down and pause at the end of sentences
review.why: Slow feels strange to the speaker but normal to the listener. Pauses let people catch up.

review.q: Which visual aid best supports the point that some dinosaurs were as long as a bus?
choices: A drawing of a dinosaur next to a school bus
review.why: The drawing shows the size comparison. The others decorate but do not help the point.

review.q: Why would Elena describe tamale dough differently to kindergartners than to her class?
choices: Kindergartners are not a real audience
A different audience knows different things
review.why: Audience changes your words. Little kids do not know what ground corn is, so she used play dough.
